title: The `print` statement only counts the lines that are actually displayed on the screen.
body: `print` is an operation that displays a value on the screen. Even if a value is stored in a variable, it will not appear on the screen unless you use `print`.
detail: Conversely, if there are multiple `print` statements, the output will span multiple lines. `print(x + 1)` is not code that changes the value of `x`; rather, it reads the value of `x` and displays the result of the calculation. When working on output problems, first check how many times `print` is executed and what the values inside each `print` statement are.

title: print: Storing expressions and variables are different
when_to_show: When you get confused between `print(x + 1)` and `x = x + 1`
body: print(x + 1) displays the result of the calculation but does not assign a new value to x. x = x + 1 calculates the expression on the right and then assigns the result back to x on the left.
detail: Although the two lines look similar, they produce different results. Beginners might mistakenly assume that if they see 3 on the screen, x has also changed to 3. When reading code, start by distinguishing between screen output and variable assignment.

title: The value received as input is initially a string.
when_to_show: When reviewing input, str, type conversion
body: Even if the user enters a value that looks like a number using `input()`, it is initially a string.
detail: Therefore, if you want to perform `age + 1` after `age = input()`, you need to convert it using something like `int(age)`. Although '3' and 3 look similar on the screen, they behave differently. In input-related problems, you must first check whether the value received via `input()` is still a string or has already been converted to an `int` or `float`.

title: Input validation comes before conversion
body: If we assume that users always enter valid numbers, the program could easily crash. `int(text)` succeeds only when `text` is in numerical format.
detail: Therefore, in real-world apps, we first check if the input is an empty string or handle conversion failures using `try/except`. At the beginner level, it’s more important to understand the concept that input values are strings and require conversion before numerical calculations than to focus on perfect validation. This card isn’t meant to provide the answer to a problem right away; rather, it’s reading material designed to help beginners repeatedly practice how to read Python code.

title: int, float, and str change how values behave
when_to_show: When reviewing int, float, str, type
body: int('3') converts the string '3' into the integer 3. float('3.5') converts it into a value suitable for floating-point calculations.
detail: str(3) converts the number 3 into a string that can be concatenated like text. Conversion functions do more than just change the appearance; they alter how the value behaves in subsequent operations. You should check the data type before and after a calculation.

title: Even if it looks like a number, if it contains quotation marks, it is a string.
when_to_show: When distinguishing between string addition and numeric addition
body: '2' + '3' is not 5, but '23'. If you use quotes, Python treats it as a string rather than a number.
detail: Conversely, 2 + 3 is numerical addition, so it equals 5. Since both may appear to be numbers on the screen, be sure to check your code for quotation marks when solving problems. This habit alone will significantly reduce many beginner mistakes.

title: A comparison expression returns either True or False.
body: "score >= 60" is not code that directly outputs a score; rather, it is a comparison expression that returns either True or False. This boolean value determines which block of code will be executed in the if statement.
detail: While `print(score >= 60)` may display True or False on the screen, `if score >= 60:` does not display anything on the screen; it simply branches the flow of execution. You must distinguish the role of the comparison expression when reading the code. This card is not intended to provide the answer to a problem directly; rather, it is reading material designed to help beginners repeatedly practice how to read Python code.

title: "if active:" is code that uses the value of "active" as a condition.
body: A statement can function as a conditional even without a comparison operator, as in `if active:`. If `active` evaluates to `True`, the `if` block is executed; if it evaluates to `False`, it is skipped.
detail: In beginner-level problems, you should first identify where `active` is defined and what value it has been assigned. Don’t assume a value is `True` just because the variable name sounds plausible; instead, follow the actual value that was assigned to it. This card is not intended to reveal the correct answer to a problem immediately; rather, it is a reading exercise designed to help beginners repeatedly practice how to read Python code.

title: The if/elif/else statements are evaluated one by one from the top down.
body: The `if, elif, else` structure evaluates conditions from top to bottom. Once the first block that evaluates to `True` is executed, the remaining `elif` and `else` blocks are not executed.
detail: Therefore, even though `score >= 60` is `True` when `score` is 85, if the `score >= 80` condition appears earlier in the code, the execution flows to the `80` condition. In problems with multiple conditions, you must always check the order of the conditions. This card is not intended to provide the answer to a problem immediately; rather, it is a reading resource designed to help beginners repeatedly practice reading Python code.

title: Indentation indicates which lines do not meet the condition.
body: Python uses indentation instead of curly braces to delimit code blocks. Lines indented under an `if` statement are executed only when the condition is true.
detail: Lines that are no longer indented are outside the conditional block and can be executed in the subsequent flow regardless of the condition’s outcome. In output exercises, the reason there are more or fewer `print` statements than expected is usually because you missed an indentation boundary. This card is not intended to provide the correct answer immediately, but rather to serve as reading material that helps beginners repeatedly practice how to read Python code.

title: A `for` loop iterates through a list of values, processing them one by one.
when_to_show: When looking at the code "for n in numbers,"
body: "for n in [1, 2, 3]" means that n takes the values 1, 2, and 3 in sequence. The same block of code is executed in each iteration, but the value of n changes.
detail: For the output problem, simply write down what n is in each iteration. For objects that can hold multiple values—such as lists, strings, and `range`—the `for` loop retrieves those values one by one and passes them to the body of the loop. This card is not intended to provide the immediate answer to a problem; rather, it is a reading exercise designed to help beginners repeatedly practice reading Python code.

title: For cumulative variables, the initial value before the loop is important.
when_to_show: When a cumulative total appears after "total = 0"
body: `total = 0` is the initial value used to start the accumulation. When `total = total + n` is executed inside the loop, the current `n` is added to the previous `total` and the result is stored back in `total`.
detail: The final result varies depending on whether the initial value is 0 or 1, an empty string, or an empty list. For accumulation problems, we examine the initial value before the loop, the changes during the loop, and the output value after the loop. This card is not intended to provide the answer to the problem immediately, but rather serves as reading material to help beginners repeatedly practice reading Python code.

title: When using a `while` loop, you need to consider both the condition and the update together.
body: A `while` loop repeats as long as the condition is `True`. Therefore, you must check whether there is a line of code within the loop that updates the condition.
detail: If there is no update—such as `i = i + 1`—the condition may remain `True`, causing the loop to never end. When analyzing a `while` problem, read it in the following order: the initial value of `i`, the condition check, the execution of the body, and the condition check again after the update. This card is not intended to provide the answer to a problem immediately, but rather serves as reading material to help beginners repeatedly practice reading Python code.

title: "break" and "continue" change the flow of a loop
body: `break` terminates the entire loop. `continue` skips only the remainder of the current iteration and moves on to the next one.
detail: Although these two keywords may seem similar, they produce significantly different results. When solving a problem, mark the point where you encounter a `break` as the exit from the loop, and when you encounter a `continue`, check whether the `print` or `append` statements below it are executed in that iteration. This card is not intended to provide the immediate answer to a problem; rather, it is a reading exercise designed to help beginners repeatedly practice reading Python code.

title: Lists remember the order of their values.
body: A list contains multiple values in order. The first value has index 0, and the second value has index 1.
detail: `items[1]` does not refer to the number 1; rather, it is an expression that retrieves the second value. When working with lists, you must not confuse the values themselves with their index numbers. Since the indices may change after using `append` or `insert`, you should reevaluate the list after making changes.

title: `append` adds a value to the end of a list
body: `items.append(x)` adds `x` to the end of the `items` list. It’s better to think of `append` as an operation that modifies the list itself, rather than a function that returns a new list.
detail: That’s why if you run `print(items)` after `append`, you’ll see the added value. Using `append` inside a loop is a common pattern for creating a result list. When used with a conditional statement, it collects only the values that satisfy the condition.

title: len counts the number of values, but it is different from index
body: `len(items)` returns the number of elements in a list. `items[0]` retrieves the first element.
detail: Both are related to lists, but they serve different purposes. For a list with a length of 3, the last index is 2, not 3. Beginners often make mistakes by using the result of `len` directly as an index.

title: A dictionary looks up a value based on a key.
when_to_show: When you see an expression like `data['name']`,
body: A dictionary looks up a value based on a key. This card is designed to reinforce your understanding of how to read keys in actual data code, within the broader concept of dictionaries.
detail: For example, data where multiple items are grouped by labels—such as API responses, JSON, configuration settings, and student grade sheets—is often represented as a dictionary. data['name'] reads the value associated with the "name" key, while scores.get('kim') retrieves the value if the "kim" key exists and handles the case safely if it does not. If you reassign a value to the same key, that key’s value changes, so the final value may differ from the initial one.

title: `get` safely handles keys that do not exist
body: dict.get returns None or a chosen default instead of raising for a missing key. It fits an accumulator such as counts.get(ch, 0), where missing means zero, but it should not hide a required key.
detail: Define whether absence is valid and what the default means.

title: "keys," "values," and "items" are different ways of looking at a dictionary
when_to_show: When reviewing dict, keys, values, items
body: "keys" refers to the list of keys, "values" refers to the list of values, and "items" is used when referring to key-value pairs.
detail: The statement `for key, value in data.items():` iterates through each pair, assigning the key and value to separate variables. When solving dictionary iteration problems, you must first determine what exactly is being iterated over. The meaning of the code changes depending on whether you’re iterating only over keys, only over values, or over both.

title: `split` splits a string into a list
body: `split` is a method that splits a string into multiple parts and creates a list.
detail: `text.split(",")` splits the string at commas, and if you omit the delimiter, as in `text.split()`, it splits the string at whitespace characters. Since the result is a list rather than a single string, you can access elements using an index (e.g., `parts[0]`) or iterate over them using a `for` loop (e.g., `for part in parts:`). The most important point to note is the change in data type before and after the `split` operation.

title: `strip` removes leading and trailing spaces
body: `strip` removes leading and trailing whitespace or line breaks from a string. When reading a line from a file, a line break may be appended at the end, and user input may contain leading or trailing whitespace.
detail: `text.strip()` creates a new, trimmed string. To apply the changes to the original variable, you must reassign it, like `text = text.strip()`. Always check where the result of a string method is assigned.

title: The `join` function concatenates a list of strings into a single string.
body: `join` is a method that combines multiple strings into a single string. Its syntax is not `list.join(...)`, but rather `separator_string.join(list_of_strings)`.
detail: For example, `"-".join(["a", "b", "c"])` produces `"a-b-c"`. The separator string is inserted between each element, and the result is a single string, not a list. A common mistake made by beginners is thinking of `join` as an operation that modifies a list, like `append`.

title: A function consists of an input, a processing step, and an output.
body: Functions typically take input, process it internally, and return a result. A “parameter” is the name used for an input value within a function, while an “argument” is the actual value passed when the function is called.
detail: The “return” statement sends the result of the processing back to the caller. When working on function problems, first locate the call line, map which arguments correspond to which parameters, and then trace the return value. This card is not intended to provide the answer to a problem immediately; rather, it is a reading guide designed to help beginners repeatedly practice reading Python code.

title: Separating `return` and `print` makes functions easier to understand
body: Separating `return` and `print` makes functions easier to understand.
detail: This card is a beginner-level reading practice card designed to help you train yourself to identify the correct answer when you encounter `print` and `return` together within the same function while solving actual problems. `print` displays a value on the screen, while `return` returns a value to the caller. A function that only has `print` and no `return` may display a value on the screen, but the result of the call may be `None`.

title: Scope is a way of distinguishing between names inside and outside a function.
when_to_show: When there are variables with the same name inside and outside a function
body: Scope is a way to distinguish between names inside and outside a function.
detail: This card takes the concept a step further than the “local variable” card; it helps you practice determining which scope’s name to use when the same name appears in multiple locations. Just because you set `x = 3` inside a function doesn’t mean the outer `x` is always affected. Names created within a function are typically looked up first within the function’s internal scope, and to pass a value to the outside, you must check if there is a `return` statement.

title: File processing is different from screen output.
when_to_show: When You Confuse `write` and `print` in Files
body: f.write('hi') writes "hi" to a file. This does not mean that "hi" will appear on the screen.
detail: To display it on the screen, you need to use print('hi'). In file-related problems, you must distinguish between the values stored in the file and those printed to the screen. `read` retrieves the contents of a file as a string, and `write` writes a string to a file.

title: The try/except statement separates the normal flow from the failure flow.
body: Code preceded by `try` is executed first. If it succeeds, the `except` block is not executed.
detail: If it fails and the error type matches the `except` clause, the `except` block is executed. `int('7')` succeeds, but `int('x')` may raise a `ValueError`. When working on exception handling problems, you should analyze the code by separating the two flow paths: what values remain when everything works normally, and what default values are assigned when an error occurs.

title: Class code distinguishes between design diagrams and actual objects.
body: Executing a class statement creates a class object. Calling Dog() normally creates an instance through __new__ and initializes it through __init__; self refers to the instance receiving a method call.
detail: Separate class definition, instance creation, attribute assignment, and method calls.

title: Debugging is the process of comparing expected values with actual values.
body: Debugging isn’t about scolding yourself for writing incorrect code; it’s the process of finding where the actual values differ from what you expected.
detail: Beginners can solve many problems simply by inserting `print` statements to check variable values. Inside loops, observe how values change with each iteration; inside functions, check the parameters and return values. This card isn’t meant to give you the answer right away; rather, it’s a reading guide designed to help beginners repeatedly practice reading Python code.

title: Beginner Code Reading Starts with a Checklist
body: When looking at a mixed problem, first find the output line. Next, trace back through the variables and function calls required for the output.
detail: If there are conditional statements, select only the blocks that are actually executed; if there are loops, note how the values change with each iteration. For lists and dictionaries, check the final remaining values. Just by following this order, code you’ve never seen before becomes much less complicated.

title: Link to external sources using links and summaries rather than copying the content.
when_to_show: When reviewing external resource, license, reading
body: While good educational websites and official documentation can be helpful for learning, copying long passages of content directly into the app can lead to copyright and quality control issues.
detail: A safe approach is to write the internal explanations yourself and link external materials to cards that include the title, source, link, difficulty level, related concepts, and reasons why they’re worth reading. This way, learners gain access to more reading material, and the app can maintain the quality of its own explanations. These cards are not meant to provide immediate answers to problems; rather, they serve as reading material to help beginners repeatedly practice reading Python code.
